periods.analysis: We are starting this run from a strong, resident-facing base: Library Visits per Capita met target exactly at 0.45 visits, After-School Program Capacity was 90.7%, and Program Cost Recovery was 46.6%. Those numbers tell me families are using the system and that access is being delivered without leaning too heavily on the General Fund. The Greenway, North Pier, and East Harbor branches all benefited from the late-summer “Read, Play, Eat” schedule, while recreation staff kept after-school rosters full at Bayview, Mercado, and Juniper centers. I am pleased, but I am not treating 0.45 visits as a cushion; it is the floor we promised residents.
periods.recommendations: Hold the current after-school staffing pattern through October and keep waitlist calls centralized through RecTrac so seats do not sit empty between sessions. Extend the “Read, Play, Eat” model to two additional library-recreation pairs, starting with South Landing Library and Tidelands Community Center. Keep fee waivers available for qualifying families while asking program managers to review supply purchasing and instructor contracts to sustain cost recovery above 40%.

periods.analysis: The fall quarter shows how much Harborview residents respond when services are easy to reach: Library Visits per Capita rose from 0.45 visits to 0.53 visits. After-School Program Capacity eased slightly from 90.7% to 89.9%, still comfortably above the 85% target, as we held a few slots open for mid-year school referrals. Program Cost Recovery moved down from 46.6% to 42.3%, which is still green and expected with holiday events, free winter break camps, and higher temporary staffing at the Central Library makerspace. The story is positive, but the margin on cost recovery is the watch item I want us to manage with care.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the extended evening and Saturday library hours at Central, East Harbor, and North Pier through the winter reading cycle because the visit lift is real. Ask each community center to run a weekly vacancy sweep against the school referral list so the 89.9% capacity level does not soften further. For cost recovery, complete a January review of vendor invoices for Winter Lights, youth basketball officials, and mobile library fuel so we protect access while rebuilding margin.

periods.analysis: This quarter held the gains we made in the fall: Library Visits per Capita slipped only slightly from 0.53 visits to 0.52 visits, which is strong for a cold-weather quarter after the holiday peak. After-School Program Capacity moved from 89.9% to 88.7%, still green, with the decline tied mostly to attendance churn in the Roosevelt and Seaport elementary cohorts. Program Cost Recovery improved from 42.3% to 45.1% as winter swim lessons, adult ESL room rentals, and youth league fees came in cleanly. I see a healthy system here: steady access, disciplined pricing, and no retreat from our equity commitments.
periods.recommendations: Keep the library outreach calendar focused on high-use family windows, especially the 3:00 to 6:00 p.m. block at Central and the airport corridor branches. Direct after-school coordinators at Roosevelt, Seaport, and Bayview to make two-contact follow-ups within 48 hours of repeated absences so paid and subsidized seats remain active. Continue the quarterly fee-waiver audit and reinvest any cost recovery over plan into transportation vouchers for low-income program participants.

periods.analysis: Spring brought a more mixed but still green result: Library Visits per Capita moved down from 0.52 visits to 0.45 visits, landing exactly on target. After-School Program Capacity declined from 88.7% to 88%, which remains above the 85% target but reflects the usual spring sports and testing-season pull. Program Cost Recovery strengthened from 45.1% to 47.8%, helped by aquatics registration at Harborview Natatorium and early summer camp deposits. The resident outcome is still good, but the library visit number tells me we need to refresh the invitation before summer, not after.
periods.recommendations: Launch the summer library card push two weeks earlier, using school backpack flyers, airport employee newsletters, and pop-up signups at Ferry Plaza. Preserve after-school capacity by converting unfilled late-spring seats into short-session homework and recreation blocks at Mercado and Tidelands. Maintain the aquatics and camp registration controls that lifted recovery to 47.8%, while setting aside scholarship capacity before popular sessions sell out.

periods.analysis: The summer reset worked: Library Visits per Capita rose from 0.45 visits to 0.47 visits, and After-School Program Capacity climbed from 88% to 91.5%. Program Cost Recovery eased from 47.8% to 45.5%, still safely green, as we absorbed more scholarship use and added heat-response programming during July. Crews and branch teams did good practical work here, including the BookBike route along Harbor Line bus stops and the expanded teen lab hours at South Landing. This is the kind of green I like best: more residents reached, with the budget still in balance.
periods.recommendations: Keep the BookBike and pop-up library route on Tuesdays and Thursdays through September, then compare card signups by stop before deciding on winter service. Protect the 91.5% capacity gain by opening waitlist-to-enrollment calls 10 days before each after-school cycle, not the Friday before. Continue heat-response recreation partnerships with Public Health, but code those costs consistently so program managers can see what is access investment versus recoverable program expense.

periods.analysis: We built on the summer momentum in the places that matter most to residents: Library Visits per Capita rose from 0.47 visits to 0.54 visits. After-School Program Capacity stayed very strong, moving only slightly from 91.5% to 91.2%, with stable rosters at Juniper, Bayview, and East Harbor. Program Cost Recovery moved down from 45.5% to 43.1%, still above the 40% target, reflecting free family literacy nights and added custodial coverage for evening branch use. I am comfortable with that tradeoff because the access gain is clear, but we should not let event costs drift without a plan.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the family literacy nights at Central, North Pier, and East Harbor because they are translating directly into visits. Have recreation supervisors lock January rosters before winter break and pre-authorize substitutes for the five highest-enrollment after-school sites. For cost recovery, create a standard event-cost template for custodial, security, supplies, and instructor time so free programs remain intentional rather than accidental.

periods.analysis: After a very strong fall, Library Visits per Capita moved from 0.54 visits to 0.51 visits, which is a modest seasonal step-down and still well above target. After-School Program Capacity declined from 91.2% to 88.5%, remaining green as some families changed schedules after the semester break. Program Cost Recovery improved from 43.1% to 44.8%, helped by winter aquatics, pickleball permits at Shoreline Courts, and steadier room rentals at Mercado. The through-line is reassuring: residents are still showing up, and we are getting better at matching program costs to demand.
periods.recommendations: Use the semester-break enrollment data to identify sites with churn above 5% and require a corrective seat-fill plan from those coordinators. Maintain the winter aquatics and court-permit schedule that improved recovery to 44.8%, and test one additional Sunday block at Shoreline Courts if staffing holds. Keep library outreach tied to practical resident needs, including tax-prep appointments, job-search labs, and multilingual story times.

periods.analysis: By spring, Library Visits per Capita moved down from 0.51 visits to 0.45 visits, again landing exactly on the target rather than below it. After-School Program Capacity improved from 88.5% to 89.1%, showing that the seat-fill work after semester break helped. Program Cost Recovery rose from 44.8% to 47.2%, supported by early summer camp deposits, aquatics renewals, and tighter event-cost coding. Over eight quarters, this objective has stayed green because the teams treated access as an operating discipline, not a slogan.
periods.recommendations: Do not accept 0.45 visits as the new normal; repeat the early summer library card push and add outreach at the seaport hiring hall, airport employee center, and three high-absenteeism school catchments. Keep the after-school vacancy protocol in place through the first month of summer transition programming so the 89.1% capacity level continues to rise. Use the stronger 47.2% cost recovery to fund targeted scholarships and transportation supports, while preserving the purchasing controls that produced the improvement.

periods.analysis: Library visits per capita narrowly exceeded target at 0.46 against 0.45, while after-school capacity was 81.4% against 85% and cost recovery was 37.3% against 40%. Riverside branch renovation remains at 70% and is past its October 9 end date. Residents can use existing services, but the unfinished branch work must not be described as a completed access improvement.
periods.recommendations: Prioritize a site-level capacity and waitlist review, and confirm a revised Riverside schedule with the project owner. Show the open services and the delayed renovation as separate items in the briefing book.
